phy_edx.12.0.summary: When a conductor and a magnetic field move relative to each other, the conductor **cuts magnetic field lines** and a **potential difference is induced** across it; if the conductor is part of a complete circuit, this drives an **induced current**. This is **electromagnetic induction**. In the lab you show it by moving a magnet into or out of a coil connected to a sensitive ammeter (or moving a wire between magnetic poles); in power stations a turbine spins a large magnet (electromagnet) inside fixed coils so a current is generated continuously.

core.p: Electromagnetic induction is producing a potential difference (and so a current, if the circuit is complete) in a conductor because of **relative movement** between the conductor and a magnetic field. The key idea is that the conductor must **cut** (or experience a change in) magnetic field lines.
bullets: A **potential difference (p.d.) is induced** across the ends of the conductor.
If the conductor is part of a **complete circuit**, an **induced current** flows.
No movement (or no change in field) means **no induced p.d.** and no current.
It does not matter which one moves: magnet moving past a still wire, or wire moving past a still magnet, both work.
This is the reverse of the motor effect: there, current plus field gives movement; here, movement plus field gives a p.d.

callouts.p: A potential difference is induced across a conductor when it experiences a change in magnetic field, for example when it moves relative to a magnetic field and cuts field lines.

core.p: The p.d. is only induced while field lines are being cut, i.e. while the magnetic field through the conductor is **changing**. A magnet sitting still inside a coil produces a field through it, but that field is not changing, so nothing is induced.
bullets: Moving magnet, still coil: induced p.d.
Still magnet, moving coil: induced p.d.
Both moving at the **same velocity**: no relative movement, so no p.d.
Moving a wire **parallel** to the field lines: no lines are cut, so no p.d.
Maximum effect when the wire moves at **right angles** to the field lines.

callouts.p: A strong magnet held still inside a coil gives a reading of zero. Students often say a current flows because the magnet is there; the mark is for saying there is no movement, so no field lines are cut.

core.p: The classic small-scale demonstration uses a bar magnet, a coil of insulated wire (a solenoid) and a **sensitive ammeter** or **centre-zero galvanometer** connected across the coil to make a complete circuit.
bullets: Connect the two ends of the coil to a centre-zero meter so readings either side of zero can be seen.
Push the N pole of the magnet **into** the coil: the needle **deflects** one way.
Hold the magnet **still** inside the coil: the needle returns to **zero**.
Pull the magnet **out**: the needle deflects the **opposite way**.
Push the S pole in: the needle deflects the opposite way to the N pole going in.
Move the magnet faster: the deflection is **larger** (but lasts a shorter time).

callouts.p: A centre-zero meter shows the direction of the current as well as its size, so you can show the current reverses when the motion reverses.

core.h: Lab method 2: wire between magnetic poles
core.p: A single straight wire connected to a sensitive meter can be moved up and down between the poles of a U-shaped (horseshoe) magnet or two flat magnets on a yoke.
bullets: Move the wire **across** the field (at right angles to the field lines): a small p.d. is induced and the needle flicks.
Reverse the direction of movement: the needle flicks the other way.
Move the wire **along** the field lines (from N towards S): no deflection.
Stop the wire: no deflection.
The effect is small with one wire, which is why a very sensitive meter is needed and why coils are used in practice.

core.h: What the meter shows and why
core.p: The pattern of readings is the evidence for electromagnetic induction. Learn it as a set of rules linking the motion to the reading.
bullets: Reading only appears **during** movement.
Reversing the direction of movement **reverses** the current.
Reversing the pole (S instead of N) **reverses** the current.
Reversing both movement and pole gives the **original** direction.
Faster movement means field lines are cut **at a greater rate**, so a **bigger** p.d. and current.
Moving the magnet in and out continuously gives a current that keeps changing direction: an **alternating current**.

core.p: Edexcel mark schemes carefully separate the **induced potential difference** from the **induced current**. A p.d. is always induced when field lines are cut; a current only flows if there is a complete circuit.
bullets: Open circuit (meter disconnected): p.d. still induced, but **no current**.
Closed circuit: the induced p.d. drives an induced current.
Size of current depends on the induced p.d. and the resistance of the circuit (I = V / R).
A voltmeter across the coil would show the induced p.d. directly.

callouts.p: Movement induces a potential difference. A current flows only if the conductor is part of a complete circuit.

core.p: Induction does not create energy from nothing. The person or machine moving the magnet does **work**, and this energy is transferred **electrically** to the circuit.
bullets: Kinetic energy store of the moving magnet or wire is transferred to the circuit electrically.
When a current is induced you have to push slightly harder: the induced current makes its own magnetic field that **opposes the movement** (covered in 13.2).
If there is no current (open circuit), there is no opposing force and no electrical energy is transferred.
In the circuit, the energy is then transferred to the thermal store of the wires and meter, or to whatever device is connected.

core.h: Large scale: generating electricity in power stations
core.p: Almost all mains electricity is produced by electromagnetic induction in **generators**. The principle is exactly the lab experiment, scaled up: a magnetic field and coils of wire move relative to each other continuously.
bullets: In most power stations a **turbine** is turned, e.g. by high-pressure **steam** (from burning fossil fuels, nuclear fission or biomass), by moving water (hydroelectric, tidal) or by wind.
The turbine is connected to a **generator** by a shaft, so the generator spins.
In large generators the **magnet (usually an electromagnet) rotates** inside **fixed (stationary) coils** of wire.
As the magnet rotates, its field lines continuously cut the coils, inducing a p.d. across them.
Because each coil sees a N pole then a S pole pass by, the induced p.d. keeps reversing: power stations generate **alternating current (a.c.)**.
In the UK the mains supply has a frequency of **50 Hz**, so the generator must rotate at a steady rate.

callouts.t: Why the magnet spins, not the coils
callouts.p: In power-station generators the heavy output coils stay still and the magnet rotates. This means the very large generated current can be taken from fixed coils by fixed connections, without sliding contacts.

core.h: Comparing lab scale and power station
core.p: The physics is identical; only the scale and engineering change.
bullets: Both need a **magnetic field**, a **conductor**, and **relative movement**.
Lab: movement by hand, tiny p.d., brief pulses of current.
Power station: continuous rotation, very large p.d. and current, steady a.c. output.

Pushed in and out by hand

core.p: Engineers want a large induced p.d. The same things that increase the meter deflection in the lab are used in real generators (detail of these factors is spec point 13.2).
bullets: **Faster** relative movement (faster rotation).
**Stronger** magnetic field (stronger magnet or electromagnet).
**More turns** on the coil, so more wire cuts the field lines.
Using an **iron core** inside the coil to concentrate the field.

core.h: Describing the experiment in a 6-mark answer
core.p: Questions often ask you to describe how to show that a current can be produced by moving a magnet, and what you would observe. Structure the answer as apparatus, method, observations and explanation.
bullets: Apparatus: coil, bar magnet, connecting leads, centre-zero ammeter/galvanometer.
Method: connect coil to meter; move magnet into coil, hold still, pull out; repeat faster and with the other pole.
Observations: deflection only while moving; opposite deflection for opposite motion or pole; bigger when faster.
Explanation: magnet's field lines are cut by the coil, inducing a p.d.; the complete circuit lets an induced current flow.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward: relative movement, cuts field lines, induced potential difference, induced current, complete circuit, reverses direction.

analogy.p: Think of the field lines as tightly stretched strings and the wire as your finger. Only when your finger **moves across** the strings do they make a sound (an induced p.d.); resting your finger on them, or sliding it along a string, makes nothing. Strum faster and you hit more strings per second, so the effect is bigger. Strum the other way and the sound pattern reverses. Where it breaks down: field lines are not real physical objects and nothing is plucked; the p.d. is due to the changing magnetic field acting on free electrons in the conductor, and the induced current also exerts a force that opposes your motion, which strings do not do.

terms.d: Producing a potential difference across a conductor when it experiences a changing magnetic field, e.g. by relative movement between conductor and magnet.
The p.d. produced across a conductor by electromagnetic induction.
The current that flows when an induced p.d. acts in a complete circuit.
Movement of the magnet and conductor compared with each other; either or both may move, but not at the same velocity.
A conductor moving across (not along) magnetic field lines, which causes a p.d. to be induced.
Region around a magnet or current-carrying conductor where a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force.
A conductor wound into many turns; used because each turn adds to the induced p.d.
A sensitive meter with zero in the middle of its scale that shows both size and direction of a small current.
An unbroken conducting path through which current can flow.
A device that transfers kinetic energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction.
A set of blades turned by steam, water or wind, connected to the shaft of a generator.
A coil carrying current, often around an iron core, that acts as a magnet; used as the rotating magnet in large generators.
A current that repeatedly reverses direction; produced by power station generators.
The number of complete cycles of the a.c. per second; 50 Hz in the UK.

mistakes.w: A current flows when the magnet is inside the coil.
mistakes.r: A p.d. is induced only while there is relative movement; a stationary magnet gives zero reading.

mistakes.w: The magnet gives the coil its electricity / electrons come from the magnet.
mistakes.r: The movement causes the conductor to cut field lines, inducing a p.d. that drives the free electrons already in the wire.

mistakes.w: Moving the wire up and down along the field lines makes a current.
mistakes.r: The wire must cut field lines; moving parallel to the field induces nothing.

mistakes.w: A current is always induced when a conductor moves in a field.
mistakes.r: A p.d. is induced; a current flows only if the conductor is in a complete circuit.

mistakes.w: Pulling the magnet out gives a current in the same direction.
mistakes.r: Reversing the direction of movement reverses the direction of the induced p.d. and current.

mistakes.w: In a power station the coils spin inside the magnet.
mistakes.r: In large power station generators the magnet (electromagnet) rotates inside fixed coils.

mistakes.w: The turbine produces the electricity.
mistakes.r: The turbine turns the generator; the generator produces the p.d. by electromagnetic induction.

mistakes.w: Moving faster makes the current last longer.
mistakes.r: Moving faster gives a larger induced p.d. and current, because field lines are cut at a greater rate.

exam.q: State what is meant by electromagnetic induction.
model: A potential difference is induced in a conductor when it moves relative to / cuts a magnetic field (or the field through it changes).
exam.tip: Say induced potential difference, not just electricity.

exam.q: A magnet is held stationary inside a coil connected to an ammeter. State the reading on the ammeter and explain why.
model: Reading is zero.
No relative movement, so no field lines are cut / magnetic field not changing, so no p.d. induced.
exam.tip: Two marks: the observation and the reason.

exam.q: A student pushes the N pole of a magnet into a coil and the meter needle moves to the right. Describe what happens to the needle when the student pulls the magnet out of the coil.
model: It deflects to the left (opposite direction).
exam.tip: Opposite movement gives opposite deflection.

exam.q: State two ways the student could make the needle deflect further.
model: Move the magnet faster.
Use a stronger magnet / use a coil with more turns.
exam.tip: Avoid vague answers like 'use a bigger magnet'; say stronger.

exam.q: A wire connected to a sensitive meter is placed between the poles of a U-shaped magnet. Explain why moving the wire parallel to the field lines gives no reading but moving it at right angles does.
model: Moving parallel, the wire does not cut field lines so no p.d. is induced.
Moving at right angles, the wire cuts field lines so a p.d. is induced and a current flows in the circuit.
exam.tip: Use the phrase cuts field lines.

exam.q: The coil is disconnected from the meter and the magnet is pushed in. State whether a potential difference is induced and whether a current flows.
model: A p.d. is still induced (across the ends of the coil).
No current flows because the circuit is not complete.
exam.tip: Separate p.d. from current.

exam.q: Explain why a student finds it slightly harder to push the magnet into the coil when the coil is connected to the meter than when it is disconnected.
model: The induced current produces its own magnetic field.
This field opposes the movement of the magnet, so work must be done against it (energy transferred electrically).
exam.tip: Link to energy conservation for a top answer.

exam.q: Describe how electricity is generated by a generator in a power station.
model: Steam (or water/wind) turns a turbine.
The turbine turns the generator shaft.
A magnet / electromagnet rotates inside fixed coils of wire.
The magnetic field lines are cut by the coils / field through the coils changes, inducing a p.d. (alternating), which drives a current to the grid.
exam.tip: Give the chain in order and name electromagnetic induction.

exam.q: Explain why the generator in a power station produces alternating current.
model: As the magnet rotates, the N pole then the S pole pass each coil.
So the direction of the induced p.d. reverses each half turn, giving a.c.
exam.tip: Link reversal to the poles changing.

exam.q: Describe an experiment to show that a current can be produced by the relative movement of a magnet and a coil. Include what you would observe and explain your observations.
model: Connect a coil to a sensitive centre-zero ammeter/galvanometer to form a complete circuit.
Push a bar magnet into the coil: needle deflects.
Hold magnet still: reading is zero.
Pull magnet out (or use S pole): needle deflects the opposite way.
Move magnet faster: larger deflection.

Explanation: relative movement means the coil cuts field lines, inducing a p.d. which drives a current in the complete circuit; direction depends on direction of motion/pole; size depends on rate of cutting.
exam.tip: Level-marked: include apparatus, method, observations AND explanation for top band.

worked.q: Predict the meter reading in each case, given that pushing the N pole into the coil gives a deflection of +4 divisions: (a) S pole pushed in at the same speed (b) N pole pulled out at the same speed (c) coil moved towards a still N pole at the same speed (d) magnet and coil moved together in the same direction at the same speed.
steps: (a) Changing the pole reverses the direction, same speed gives same size: -4.
(b) Reversing the direction of motion reverses the direction: -4.
(c) Only relative movement matters; this is the same as the N pole moving in: +4.
(d) No relative movement, so no field lines cut: 0.

worked.q: A coil connected to a meter has a total resistance of 2.0 ohms. Moving a magnet into it induces a p.d. of 0.012 V. Calculate the induced current. What would the current be if the meter were disconnected?
steps: Use V = I x R, so I = V / R.
If disconnected, the circuit is not complete: the p.d. is still induced but the current is 0.
worked.ans: 6 mA (0.006 A) when connected; 0 A when disconnected, although the 0.012 V p.d. is still induced.

worked.q: Model answer: explain how a wind turbine generates a current.
steps: Wind turns the blades (kinetic energy store of the air transferred).
The blades turn a shaft connected to a generator.
In the generator a magnet rotates relative to coils of wire.
The coils cut the magnetic field lines, so a p.d. is induced (electromagnetic induction).
The coils are connected to a complete circuit, so an alternating current flows.
worked.ans: Moving air turns the turbine, which spins the generator, producing relative movement between magnet and coils that induces a p.d. and an alternating current.

phy_edx.12.1.summary: The **size** of an induced potential difference depends on how quickly the magnetic field lines are cut: it increases with the **speed of movement**, the **strength of the magnetic field** and the **number of turns on the coil**. The **direction** of the induced p.d. reverses if you reverse the **direction of movement** or the **polarity of the magnet**. Whenever an induced current flows, it creates its **own magnetic field that opposes the original change** (the movement that caused it), which is why work must be done to generate electricity.

core.h: Quick recap: what is being induced
core.p: When a conductor and a magnetic field move relative to each other, the conductor cuts field lines and a **potential difference is induced** across it. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, an **induced current** flows. This spec point is about what decides how big that p.d. is, which way it acts, and what the resulting current does.
bullets: An induced p.d. needs a **change** in the magnetic field experienced by the conductor.
No relative movement means no induced p.d. at all.
The p.d. exists even in an open circuit; a current needs a complete circuit.
Bigger induced p.d. gives a bigger induced current for the same circuit resistance.

core.p: Moving the magnet or conductor **faster** means field lines are cut **at a greater rate** (more lines per second), so the induced p.d. is **larger**.
bullets: Push the magnet in twice as fast: bigger deflection on the meter, but for a shorter time.
In a generator: spin the coil or magnet faster, get a larger p.d.
Speed affects the size only, not the direction.
Zero speed (stationary) gives zero p.d.

callouts.p: Every size factor works the same way: it increases the rate at which field lines are cut, so the induced p.d. increases.

core.h: Factor 2: strength of the magnetic field
core.p: A **stronger magnetic field** has field lines packed more closely together. Moving through it at the same speed cuts more lines per second, so the induced p.d. is larger.
bullets: Use a **stronger magnet** (not just a bigger one).
Use an **electromagnet** with a larger current.
Put a **soft iron core** inside the coil to concentrate the field.
Bring the magnet closer: the field is stronger near the poles.

callouts.p: Write 'stronger magnet', not 'bigger magnet'. A bigger magnet is not necessarily stronger and will not get the mark.

core.h: Factor 3: number of turns on the coil
core.p: Each turn of a coil has its own small p.d. induced across it. The turns are connected in series, so the p.d.s **add up**. **More turns** gives a **larger total induced p.d.**
bullets: Double the turns (same speed, same magnet) roughly doubles the induced p.d.
This is why generators and microphones use coils, not single wires.
A single straight wire gives only a tiny p.d.
More turns also means more wire, so more resistance; the p.d. still increases.

bullets: **Speed** of movement (faster = bigger).
**Strength** of the magnetic field (stronger = bigger).
**Number of turns** on the coil (more = bigger).

core.h: The induced field opposes the change
core.p: When an induced current flows in a coil, the coil becomes an **electromagnet** with its own magnetic field. The direction of the induced current is always such that this field **opposes the original change** (the movement) that produced it.
bullets: N pole **pushed in**: the near end of the coil becomes a **N pole**, which **repels** the incoming magnet.
N pole **pulled out**: the near end of the coil becomes a **S pole**, which **attracts** the magnet, resisting it leaving.
Either way, the coil tries to stop the relative movement.
For a straight wire in a generator or a moving conductor, the induced current feels a force (the motor effect) that acts **against** the direction of motion.
This rule is known as Lenz's law, though Edexcel only needs the idea, not the name.

callouts.p: The induced current produces a magnetic field that opposes the original change (the movement of the magnet or conductor) that caused it.

core.p: The opposing field is a consequence of **conservation of energy**. Electrical energy is transferred to the circuit, so work must be done on the system by whatever is pushing the magnet or turning the generator.
bullets: If the induced field **helped** the movement, the magnet would speed up by itself and produce energy from nothing, which is impossible.
So you feel a resistive force: you must do **work** against the opposing magnetic force.
The work done is transferred **electrically** to the circuit (then to thermal stores, devices, etc.).
Larger induced current means a larger opposing force, so a generator supplying more current is harder to turn.
If the circuit is **open**, no current flows, there is no opposing field and the magnet moves freely.

callouts.p: In explain questions, link opposition to energy: work done against the opposing force is transferred electrically to the circuit.

core.h: Working out the poles step by step
core.p: Exam questions often give a diagram and ask which pole forms at one end of the coil, or which way the current flows. Use this routine.
bullets: Step 1: identify the change (which pole, approaching or leaving).
Step 2: approaching, the coil end facing it becomes the **same pole** (repel).
Step 3: leaving, the coil end facing it becomes the **opposite pole** (attract).
Step 4: the other end of the coil is the opposite pole to that end.
Step 5 (if needed): use the right-hand grip rule to find current direction from the pole.

callouts.p: Coming in: repel. Going out: attract. The coil always tries to keep things as they were.

core.p: These factors explain the design of every induction device in the rest of the topic.
bullets: Generators use strong electromagnets, coils with many turns and high rotation speeds to make a large p.d.
Faster rotation in an alternator also raises the frequency of the a.c.
A cyclist's dynamo light is brighter when they pedal faster.
Turning a generator connected to a lamp is harder than when it is disconnected (opposing force).

core.p: You might be asked to plan an investigation into one factor, such as the number of turns.
bullets: Independent variable: e.g. number of turns (wind coils of 50, 100, 150 turns).
Dependent variable: maximum induced p.d., measured with a data logger or sensitive voltmeter.
Control variables: same magnet, same speed (e.g. drop the magnet from the same height through the coil), same coil diameter.
Dropping a magnet through a vertical tube coil gives a repeatable speed.
Repeat and calculate a mean; plot maximum p.d. against number of turns.

callouts.p: Pushing by hand gives an uncontrolled speed. Dropping from a fixed height is a better way to keep speed constant.

analogy.p: Imagine field lines as people standing in a crowd and the coil as you walking through. The more people you brush past each second (the induced p.d.), the bigger the effect: walk faster (speed), pack the crowd tighter (stronger field) or link arms with friends so you all brush past people at once (more turns). Turn round and walk back and the direction reverses. And the crowd always pushes back against you, whichever way you go, so you have to do work to get through (the induced field opposes the change). Where it breaks down: field lines are not real objects, and the opposition only appears if a current flows in a complete circuit, whereas a crowd pushes back regardless.

Name for the rule that an induced current always acts to oppose the change producing it.
A coil carrying a current, which has a magnetic field like a bar magnet.
Iron placed inside a coil to concentrate the magnetic field, increasing the induced p.d.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed; the electrical energy produced comes from work done against the opposing force.
Energy transferred when a force moves an object; here, done against the opposing magnetic force.

mistakes.r: Use a stronger magnet (stronger magnetic field).

mistakes.w: Move the magnet slower to get a bigger p.d. because it stays in the coil longer.
mistakes.r: Move the magnet faster: field lines are cut at a greater rate, so the induced p.d. is larger.

mistakes.r: Strength, speed and number of turns change only the size; direction depends on direction of movement and the pole.

mistakes.w: When the N pole approaches, the coil becomes a S pole to attract it.
mistakes.r: The coil end becomes a N pole to repel it, opposing the movement.

mistakes.w: The induced field helps the magnet move into the coil.
mistakes.r: The induced field always opposes the change (movement) that caused it.

mistakes.w: Reversing both the pole and the movement makes the current reverse twice as much.
mistakes.r: Reversing both gives the original direction.

mistakes.w: More turns makes the p.d. smaller because of more resistance.
mistakes.r: More turns increases the induced p.d., because the p.d. in each turn adds up.

mistakes.r: No current flows in an open circuit, so there is no induced field and no opposing force.

exam.q: State two factors that affect the size of the potential difference induced when a magnet is moved into a coil.
model: Speed of movement (of magnet/coil).
Strength of the magnet / magnetic field.
Number of turns on the coil. (any two)
exam.tip: Say 'stronger', not 'bigger'.

exam.q: State one way to reverse the direction of the induced current.
model: Move the magnet in the opposite direction / use the opposite pole.
exam.tip: Not 'change the speed'.

exam.q: A student pushes the N pole into a coil, then pushes the S pole in at the same speed. Describe the difference in the meter readings.
model: Same size of deflection.
Opposite direction.
exam.tip: Comment on both size and direction.

exam.q: Explain why moving the magnet faster produces a larger induced potential difference.
model: Field lines are cut at a greater rate / magnetic field changes faster.
So a larger p.d. is induced.
exam.tip: Rate is the key word.

exam.q: The N pole of a magnet is pushed towards end X of a coil connected in a complete circuit. State the magnetic pole induced at end X and explain why.
model: N pole.
The induced current produces a field that opposes the movement, so it repels the approaching N pole.
exam.tip: Same pole to repel an approaching magnet.

exam.q: The magnet is now pulled away from end X. State and explain the pole at end X.
model: S pole.
It attracts the magnet, opposing it moving away.
exam.tip: Opposite pole to attract a leaving magnet.

exam.q: A student turns a small generator connected to a lamp. Explain why it is harder to turn when the lamp is connected than when it is disconnected.
model: With the lamp connected, an induced current flows.
The current produces a magnetic field / force that opposes the motion.
More work must be done; energy transferred electrically to the lamp. (Disconnected: no current, no opposing force.)
exam.tip: Link to energy for the third mark.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of energy, why the magnetic field of an induced current must oppose the change that produced it.
model: Electrical energy is transferred to the circuit.
This energy must come from work done by the person/machine moving the magnet.
If the field helped the motion, energy would be created from nothing, breaking conservation of energy.
exam.tip: Mention conservation of energy explicitly.

exam.q: Describe how you would investigate how the number of turns on a coil affects the induced potential difference.
model: Make coils with different numbers of turns (e.g. 50, 100, 150).
Drop the same magnet through each coil from the same height (control speed).
Measure the maximum induced p.d. with a data logger/voltmeter.
Repeat, take mean, keep magnet strength and coil size constant; plot p.d. against turns.
exam.tip: Name independent, dependent and control variables.

exam.q: Explain how the size and direction of the induced potential difference in a coil can be changed, and describe how the magnetic field of the induced current affects the movement of the magnet.
model: Size increases with greater speed of movement.
Size increases with a stronger magnetic field.
Size increases with more turns on the coil; all because field lines are cut at a greater rate.
Direction reverses if the direction of movement is reversed or the pole is reversed (both reversed gives original direction).
Induced current makes the coil an electromagnet whose field opposes the change: approaching N pole repelled (coil end N).
Leaving magnet attracted (coil end S); so work must be done, energy transferred electrically.
exam.tip: Cover size, direction and opposition to reach the top level.

worked.q: Pushing a magnet into a 100-turn coil at a certain speed induces a maximum p.d. of 0.20 V. Predict the p.d. if (a) a 300-turn coil is used at the same speed, (b) the 100-turn coil is used with the magnet moving twice as fast, (c) the S pole is used with the 100-turn coil at the original speed.
steps: (a) The p.d. in each turn adds up, so 3 times the turns gives about 3 times the p.d.: 3 x 0.20 = 0.60 V.
(b) Twice the speed cuts field lines at twice the rate: 2 x 0.20 = 0.40 V.
(c) Same speed and turns, so same size, but opposite pole reverses direction: -0.20 V.
worked.ans: (a) about 0.60 V (b) about 0.40 V (c) 0.20 V in the opposite direction (-0.20 V).

worked.q: A magnet is dropped N pole first through a vertical coil connected to a data logger. Describe and explain the p.d.-time graph and the effect on the magnet's fall.
steps: As the N pole enters, the top of the coil becomes a N pole to oppose it: p.d. pulse in one direction.
As the magnet leaves the bottom, the coil opposes it leaving, so the current reverses: pulse in the opposite direction.
The second pulse is taller and narrower because the magnet is moving faster (it has accelerated).
Opposing forces act upwards on the magnet both times, so it falls with a slightly smaller acceleration than a free-falling magnet.
worked.ans: Two opposite pulses, the second larger and shorter; the opposing induced field slightly slows the magnet's fall.

worked.q: Model answer: why is a generator in a power station connected to a large turbine rather than just set spinning once?
steps: When the generator supplies current, the induced current creates a field that opposes the rotation.
Without a continuous driving force it would slow down and stop.
The turbine provides a continuous force, doing work against the opposing force.
This work is transferred electrically to the National Grid.
worked.ans: Because the induced current opposes the rotation, continuous work must be done by the turbine to keep the generator turning and supplying energy.

phy_edx.12.2.summary: Both **alternators** and **dynamos** are generators: a **coil rotates in a magnetic field** (or a magnet rotates near a coil), the coil cuts field lines and a **potential difference is induced** by electromagnetic induction. In an alternator the coil is connected to the external circuit through **slip rings and brushes**, so the induced p.d. reverses every half turn and the output is **alternating current (a.c.)**. In a dynamo a **split-ring commutator** swaps the connections every half turn, at the moment the p.d. reverses, so the current in the external circuit always flows in the same direction: **direct current (d.c.)**.

core.p: A simple generator is a rectangular coil of wire on an axle, placed between the poles of a magnet. Something (a turbine, a wheel, a handle) turns the axle. As the coil **rotates**, its sides **cut the magnetic field lines**, so a **potential difference is induced** across the coil.
bullets: Energy transfer: **kinetic** energy of the rotating coil transferred **electrically** to the circuit.
The faster it rotates, the faster the field lines are cut.
The two long sides of the coil do the cutting; they move in opposite directions (one up, one down), so their p.d.s add round the coil.
The ends of the coil must be connected to the outside circuit without the wires twisting up: this is the job of the **slip rings** or **commutator** with **brushes**.

callouts.p: Alternators and dynamos induce the p.d. in exactly the same way. The only difference is how the coil is connected to the external circuit.

core.h: Why the induced p.d. reverses every half turn
core.p: Each side of the coil moves **up** through the field for half a turn, then **down** for the next half. Reversing the direction of movement reverses the induced p.d., so inside the coil the p.d. is always alternating.
bullets: First half turn: left side moving up, right side moving down: p.d. in one direction.
Second half turn: left side moving down, right side moving up: p.d. reversed.
So the coil itself always produces an alternating p.d.
What reaches the external circuit depends on the slip rings or commutator.

core.h: Coil position and size of p.d.
core.p: The size of the induced p.d. depends on how quickly the coil's sides are cutting field lines at that moment, which depends on the coil's angle.
bullets: Coil **horizontal** (plane parallel to the field lines): sides move at **right angles** to the field, cutting lines fastest: **maximum p.d.**
Coil **vertical** (plane at right angles to the field lines): sides move **along** the field lines, cutting none: **p.d. is zero**.
At angles between, the p.d. is between zero and maximum.
So the output rises and falls smoothly, giving a sine-shaped graph.
The p.d. is zero and changes direction each time the coil passes the vertical position.

core.p: An **alternator** generates **alternating current**. Each end of the coil is fixed to its own complete metal ring, a **slip ring**, which turns with the coil. Stationary carbon **brushes** press on the rings and connect them to the external circuit.
bullets: Each end of the coil is **always** connected to the **same** slip ring and the same brush.
So when the induced p.d. in the coil reverses, the p.d. across the brushes reverses too.
The current in the external circuit changes direction **every half turn**.
Output: **a.c.**, a sine-wave graph with positive and negative halves.
Brushes let the rings rotate while keeping electrical contact, so the wires do not twist.

callouts.p: A generator that uses slip rings and brushes so that the induced current in the external circuit alternates in direction (a.c.).

core.p: A **dynamo** generates **direct current**. Instead of two slip rings, both ends of the coil are joined to the two halves of a single **split ring** called a **commutator**. Two brushes press on opposite sides of it.
bullets: The split ring rotates with the coil; the gaps pass the brushes every half turn.
The gaps are positioned so the swap happens when the coil is **vertical**, just as the induced p.d. passes through zero and reverses.
At that moment the connections of the coil to the external circuit are **swapped**.
The p.d. in the coil reverses, but so do the connections, so the current in the external circuit **keeps the same direction**.
Output: **d.c.**, although it is not steady: it rises and falls (a series of humps) but **never reverses**.

core.p: On an oscilloscope or p.d.-time graph the two outputs look different, even though the coils are turning in the same way.
bullets: Alternator: smooth wave above and below the axis; **p.d. reverses**.
Dynamo: the negative halves are flipped above the axis; humps all on one side.
Both reach zero twice per rotation (coil vertical).
Both have the same peak p.d. for the same coil, field and speed.
One full rotation of an alternator gives one complete cycle of a.c.

core.h: Alternator vs dynamo at a glance
core.p: Learn this comparison table; it covers most short-answer questions on this point.
bullets: Same: rotating coil, magnetic field, electromagnetic induction, brushes.
Different: slip rings vs split ring, a.c. vs d.c.

head: Feature
Alternator
Dynamo
rows: Each always joined to same brush
Swapped between brushes every half turn
Humps, all one side of axis
Old bicycle dynamo lights, simple d.c. generators

callouts.p: A dynamo has the same split-ring commutator as a d.c. motor. A motor uses current to make rotation; a dynamo uses rotation to make current.

core.p: The factors from 13.2 apply directly to a rotating coil.
bullets: **Faster rotation**: larger peak p.d. **and** a higher **frequency** (more cycles per second).
**Stronger magnetic field**: larger peak p.d., same frequency.
**More turns** on the coil: larger peak p.d., same frequency.
An **iron core** inside the coil concentrates the field: larger peak p.d.
Reversing the direction of rotation reverses the sequence of the output, but an alternator still gives a.c.

callouts.p: If asked to draw the output when the coil turns twice as fast: peaks twice as tall and twice as many cycles in the same time.

core.p: For a simple alternator one complete rotation of the coil produces one complete cycle of a.c. So the frequency of the output equals the number of rotations per second.
bullets: frequency (Hz) = number of rotations per second.
time period T = 1 / f.
UK mains a.c. is **50 Hz**, so power-station generators are controlled to rotate at a steady rate.
A 25 rotations per second coil gives 25 Hz a.c.

core.p: Large alternators, such as those in power stations, are usually built the other way round: an **electromagnet rotates** inside **fixed coils**. The relative movement is the same, so a.c. is still induced.
bullets: The large output current is taken directly from the fixed coils, avoiding sliding contacts that would spark and wear.
Only the small current for the rotating electromagnet passes through slip rings.
Car alternators also use this design; the a.c. is then converted to d.c. to charge the battery.
Edexcel may describe either design; both rely on relative motion of magnet and coil.

core.p: When the generator supplies a current, the induced current in the coil produces a magnetic field (a motor-effect force) that **opposes the rotation**. This is why a generator gets harder to turn when it is lighting a lamp.
bullets: More current drawn means a larger opposing force.
The turbine or cyclist must do more work, which is transferred electrically to the circuit.
With nothing connected (open circuit), no current flows and the coil turns easily.

core.p: A typical question asks you to explain how a generator produces a.c. or d.c. Use a clear sequence.
bullets: 1. Coil rotates in a magnetic field (turned by turbine etc.).
2. Sides of the coil cut field lines, so a p.d. is induced (electromagnetic induction).
3. Each side moves up then down, so the p.d. reverses every half turn.
4. Alternator: slip rings keep each end connected to the same brush, so output alternates (a.c.).
5. Dynamo: split-ring commutator swaps connections every half turn as the p.d. reverses, so output current is in one direction (d.c.).
6. Maximum p.d. when coil horizontal, zero when vertical; faster rotation gives larger p.d.

callouts.p: Use the exact names: slip rings, brushes, split-ring commutator. Saying 'the ring thing' or just 'commutator' for an alternator loses marks.

analogy.t: A skipping rope and a swapping referee
analogy.p: Picture the induced p.d. in the spinning coil as a skipping rope swinging up then down: inside the coil it always alternates. In an alternator the rope's ends are held by the same two people the whole time, so the people feel it go up, then down: alternating current. In a dynamo, a referee (the split-ring commutator) swaps which person holds which end every time the rope reaches the bottom of its swing, so each person always feels it pulling the same way: direct current. Where it breaks down: no physical rope is moving round the circuit; it is the direction of the induced p.d. that reverses, and the swap in a dynamo is done by the rotating split ring sliding under fixed brushes, not by a separate controller.

terms.d: A device that uses electromagnetic induction to transfer energy from a kinetic store to electrical energy.
A generator that produces alternating current, using slip rings and brushes.
A generator that produces direct current, using a split-ring commutator and brushes.
Two complete metal rings, each fixed to one end of the coil, rotating with it so each end always connects to the same brush.
A metal ring split into two halves joined to the coil ends, which reverses the coil's connections to the external circuit every half turn.
Fixed carbon contacts that press against the rotating rings to connect the coil to the external circuit.
Current that repeatedly reverses direction.
Current that flows in one direction only (its size may vary).
Inducing a p.d. across a conductor by a changing magnetic field, e.g. a coil rotating in a field.
The maximum value of the induced p.d., when the coil sides cut field lines fastest (coil parallel to field).
Number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz); equals rotations per second for a simple alternator.
Time for one complete cycle; T = 1 / f, measured in seconds.
An instrument that displays how a p.d. varies with time as a trace on a screen.
Rotating blades turned by steam, water or wind that drive the generator shaft.

mistakes.w: A dynamo produces a.c. and an alternator produces d.c.
mistakes.r: Alternator gives alternating current; dynamo gives direct current.

mistakes.w: An alternator uses a split-ring commutator.
mistakes.r: An alternator uses slip rings and brushes; a dynamo uses a split-ring commutator.

mistakes.w: The p.d. is greatest when the coil is vertical, facing the magnets.
mistakes.r: It is greatest when the coil is horizontal (parallel to field), as the sides cut field lines at the greatest rate; zero when vertical.

mistakes.w: The commutator stops the p.d. in the coil from reversing.
mistakes.r: The p.d. in the coil still reverses; the commutator reverses the connections to the external circuit at the same moment, so the output is d.c.

mistakes.w: D.c. from a dynamo is a steady, constant value.
mistakes.r: Dynamo output is in one direction but varies in size, rising and falling to zero twice each rotation.

mistakes.w: Rotating faster only increases the frequency.
mistakes.r: Rotating faster increases both the peak p.d. and the frequency.

mistakes.w: The brushes rotate with the coil.
mistakes.r: The brushes are fixed; the rings or commutator rotate and slide against them.

mistakes.w: Using a stronger magnet increases the frequency.
mistakes.r: A stronger magnet increases the peak p.d. only; frequency depends on the rotation rate.

exam.q: State the type of current produced by an alternator.
model: Alternating current (a.c.).
exam.tip: One word answers are fine for 1 mark.

exam.q: Name the part of a dynamo that allows it to produce direct current.
model: Split-ring commutator.
exam.tip: Give the full name.

exam.q: State the position of the coil, relative to the magnetic field, when the induced p.d. is (a) maximum and (b) zero.
model: (a) Plane of coil parallel to field lines (horizontal).
(b) Plane of coil perpendicular to field lines (vertical).
exam.tip: Think about whether the sides cut lines.

exam.q: Explain why the induced p.d. is zero when the coil is vertical.
model: The sides of the coil are moving parallel to / along the field lines.
So no field lines are cut (at that instant) and no p.d. is induced.
exam.tip: Key phrase: no field lines cut.

exam.q: Explain how slip rings in an alternator result in an alternating output.
model: Each end of the coil is always connected to the same slip ring/brush.
So when the induced p.d. in the coil reverses each half turn, the current in the external circuit reverses.
exam.tip: Link the fixed connection to the reversal.

exam.q: Sketch and describe how the output p.d. of an alternator changes if the coil rotates twice as fast.
model: Peak p.d. increases (doubles).
Frequency doubles / twice as many cycles in the same time (period halves).
exam.tip: Two changes: height and spacing.

exam.q: A simple alternator coil turns 30 times per second. Calculate the frequency and the time period of the a.c. output.
model: f = 30 Hz.
exam.tip: Include units.

exam.q: State two ways of increasing the peak p.d. of a dynamo without changing the speed of rotation.
model: Use a stronger magnet / magnetic field.
Use more turns on the coil / add an iron core.
exam.tip: Speed is excluded, so give the other two.

exam.q: Describe the difference between the output of an alternator and a dynamo as shown on an oscilloscope.
model: Alternator trace goes above and below the zero line (sine wave).
Dynamo trace stays on one side of the zero line (humps), falling to zero but not reversing.
exam.tip: Describe the shape relative to the zero line.

exam.q: Explain how a dynamo produces direct current. Refer to electromagnetic induction and the parts of the dynamo.
model: Coil rotates in a magnetic field (between poles of a magnet).
Sides of the coil cut field lines, inducing a p.d. (electromagnetic induction).
Each side moves up then down, so the p.d. in the coil reverses every half turn.
Coil ends are connected to a split-ring commutator; brushes connect it to the circuit.
The commutator swaps the connections every half turn, when the coil is vertical / p.d. is zero and reversing.
So current in the external circuit always flows the same way (d.c.), varying from zero to a maximum.
exam.tip: Link the timing of the swap to the p.d. reversing for the top level.

worked.q: An alternator produces an a.c. output with a peak of 6.0 V and a frequency of 20 Hz. The coil rotation rate is then increased to 40 rotations per second. Predict the new frequency, time period and peak p.d.
steps: Originally 20 Hz means 20 rotations per second (one cycle per rotation).
New frequency = 40 rotations per second = 40 Hz.
Time period T = 1 / f = 1 / 40 = 0.025 s.
Rotating twice as fast cuts field lines at twice the rate, so the peak p.d. doubles: 2 x 6.0 = 12 V.
worked.ans: Frequency 40 Hz, time period 0.025 s, peak p.d. about 12 V.

worked.q: On an oscilloscope, one complete cycle of an alternator's output covers 4 squares horizontally. The time base is set to 5 ms per square. Calculate the frequency and the rotation rate of the coil.
steps: Time period T = 4 squares x 5 ms = 20 ms = 0.020 s.
One cycle per rotation, so the coil rotates 50 times per second.

worked.q: Model answer: a simple generator has its slip rings replaced with a split-ring commutator. Explain what happens to the output.
steps: The p.d. induced in the coil still reverses every half turn.
With the commutator, the connections to the external circuit swap every half turn, when the coil is vertical and the p.d. is zero.
So the reversed p.d. is reconnected the other way round.
The current in the external circuit is now always in the same direction: the alternator has become a dynamo producing d.c. (varying size, same peak).
worked.ans: The output changes from a.c. to d.c.: same peak and timing of humps, but all on one side of the zero line.

phy_edx.12.3.summary: A **moving-coil microphone** uses **electromagnetic induction**: the pressure variations in a sound wave make a diaphragm and an attached coil vibrate in the field of a permanent magnet, inducing an alternating potential difference whose pattern matches the sound. A **loudspeaker** (or headphone) does the reverse using the **motor effect**: an alternating current in a coil in a magnetic field produces a changing force that makes a cone vibrate and push on the air, producing sound waves with the same frequency as the current.

core.p: Edexcel 13.4P (triple only) asks you to **explain the action of a microphone in converting the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current in electrical circuits, and the reverse effect as used in loudspeakers and headphones**. The two devices are built almost identically but work in opposite directions.
bullets: Microphone: **sound energy in, electrical signal out** (a transducer using electromagnetic induction)
Loudspeaker and headphones: **electrical signal in, sound out** (a transducer using the motor effect)
Both contain a **permanent magnet**, a **coil of wire** and a part that vibrates (a **diaphragm** or **cone**)
You must be able to describe the chain of cause and effect step by step, in order

callouts.p: Microphone = generator effect (movement makes current). Loudspeaker = motor effect (current makes movement).

core.p: A sound wave is a **longitudinal wave**: air particles vibrate backwards and forwards along the direction the wave travels. This creates regions of high pressure (**compressions**) and low pressure (**rarefactions**). When a sound wave hits a surface, the changing pressure pushes and pulls on it, so the surface vibrates at the **same frequency** as the sound.
bullets: Compression = higher pressure pushes the diaphragm **in**
Rarefaction = lower pressure lets the diaphragm move **out**
Louder sound = larger pressure variations = **larger amplitude** of vibration
Higher pitch = higher **frequency** = faster vibration of the diaphragm

core.p: A moving-coil (dynamic) microphone has a thin, light **diaphragm** attached to a **coil of wire**. The coil sits in the narrow gap of a **permanent magnet**, where there is a strong magnetic field. The ends of the coil are connected to the circuit (usually an amplifier).
bullets: **Diaphragm**: thin and light so that even small pressure changes make it move
**Coil**: fixed to the diaphragm, so it moves whenever the diaphragm moves
**Permanent magnet**: provides a strong, steady magnetic field across the coil
The coil is free to move **backwards and forwards** in the field

core.h: How a microphone works: step by step
core.p: This is the sequence mark schemes look for. Each step causes the next, so keep them in order.
bullets: 1. **Pressure variations** in the sound wave make the **diaphragm vibrate**
2. The **coil**, attached to the diaphragm, **vibrates** (moves backwards and forwards) too
3. The coil **moves relative to the magnetic field** of the permanent magnet, so the wire **cuts magnetic field lines**
4. A **potential difference is induced** across the ends of the coil (**electromagnetic induction**)
5. Because the coil is part of a **complete circuit**, an **induced current** flows
6. The coil changes direction each half-vibration, so the induced p.d. and current **change direction**: an **alternating** current
7. The current **varies in the same way as the pressure** of the sound wave: same frequency, and amplitude related to loudness

callouts.p: Always say the coil moves IN a magnetic field (or cuts field lines). Saying only 'the diaphragm vibrates and makes a current' loses the induction mark.

core.h: Why the current copies the sound
core.p: The induced p.d. depends on how fast the coil moves through the field and in which direction. The diaphragm follows the pressure pattern of the sound, so the coil's motion, and therefore the induced p.d., follows the same pattern. This is what makes the electrical signal a copy (an analogue) of the sound.
bullets: **Frequency**: one full vibration of the diaphragm gives one full cycle of alternating current, so the current has the **same frequency** as the sound
**Amplitude**: a louder sound moves the coil further and faster, so it cuts field lines faster and a **larger p.d.** is induced
Direction: coil moving in induces current one way; coil moving out induces current the **opposite way**
Faster cutting of field lines = larger induced p.d. (links to 13.2 factors)

callouts.p: The output of a microphone is an alternating current whose variations match the pressure variations of the sound wave.

core.p: A microphone transfers energy from the sound wave to the electrical circuit. The energy it produces is tiny, which is why the signal must be **amplified** before it can drive a loudspeaker.
bullets: Energy carried by the sound wave is transferred **mechanically** to the diaphragm and coil (kinetic energy)
Energy is then transferred **electrically** to the circuit by the induced current
Some energy is wasted as **heating** the coil (resistance) and as sound reflected from the diaphragm
The output current is very small, so an **amplifier** increases its size

core.p: A loudspeaker has a **coil** attached to a light **paper or plastic cone**. The coil sits in the strong field of a **permanent magnet**. The coil is connected to an amplifier, which supplies an **alternating current** that carries the sound signal.
bullets: **Cone**: large area so it pushes a lot of air, producing a loud sound
**Coil**: attached to the back of the cone and free to move in and out
**Permanent magnet**: gives a steady magnetic field at right angles to the wire of the coil
Headphones work in exactly the same way, with a smaller diaphragm instead of a cone

core.h: How a loudspeaker works: step by step
core.p: The loudspeaker reverses the microphone chain. Instead of movement causing a current, a current in a magnetic field causes movement: the **motor effect**.
bullets: 1. An **alternating current** from the amplifier flows through the **coil**
2. The current-carrying coil is in the **magnetic field** of the permanent magnet, so it experiences a **force** (motor effect)
3. When the current **reverses direction**, the **force reverses direction**
4. So the coil is pushed **in and out** (backwards and forwards): it **vibrates**
5. The **cone**, attached to the coil, vibrates at the **same frequency** as the current
6. The cone pushes and pulls the air, creating **compressions and rarefactions**: a **sound wave**
7. Larger current = larger force = larger vibrations = **louder** sound; higher frequency current = **higher pitch**

callouts.p: A loudspeaker does not use electromagnetic induction to make the sound. It uses the motor effect: a force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

core.h: Why an alternating current is needed
core.p: A sound wave needs the cone to move back and forth repeatedly. A steady direct current would give a steady force in one direction, so the cone would just move out once and stay there: no sound would be produced.
bullets: **d.c.**: constant force, cone pushed to one position, **no vibration, no sound** (apart from a click when switched)
**a.c.**: force keeps reversing, cone vibrates, **sound produced**
The frequency of the a.c. sets the **frequency (pitch)** of the sound
The size of the current sets the **amplitude (loudness)** of the sound

core.p: The microphone and loudspeaker are a matched pair. In fact a loudspeaker can be used as a crude microphone, because speaking into it moves the coil in the field and induces a p.d.
bullets: Same parts: magnet, coil, vibrating diaphragm or cone
Opposite direction of energy transfer
Microphone needs a **light** diaphragm to respond to small pressure changes
Loudspeaker needs a **large** cone to move lots of air

core.p: In a public address system or phone call, a microphone and a loudspeaker are linked through an amplifier. The sound pattern is carried through every stage as a varying current.
bullets: Microphone converts sound into a **small varying current**
**Amplifier** increases the size (amplitude) of the signal while keeping its **frequency and shape**
Loudspeaker converts the large varying current back into **sound**
If the signal shape is kept, the output sound is a faithful copy of the input sound

core.p: Higher-mark questions often expect you to link this point to the rest of the magnetism and induction topics.
bullets: 13.1P and 13.2: induced p.d. is larger if the coil moves **faster**, the field is **stronger**, or there are **more turns**
13.3P: like an alternator, the microphone gives **a.c.** because the coil keeps reversing direction
Topic 12 (triple): the motor effect force is given by **F = B x I x l**, so a bigger current gives a bigger force on the loudspeaker coil
Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force on the loudspeaker coil

callouts.p: For a 6 mark 'explain how a microphone and loudspeaker work' question, give both chains in order, name induction for the microphone and the motor effect for the loudspeaker, and say why the current alternates.

analogy.p: A microphone is like a trampoline with a bell rope tied to it: every time someone bounces (a sound wave pushes), the rope is pulled up and down, ringing a signal that copies the bounces exactly. A loudspeaker is the reverse: you pull the rope (the current) and the trampoline moves, pushing the air above it. Where it breaks down: there is no rope; the link is made by a magnetic field, and in the microphone it is the coil cutting field lines that creates the p.d., not a mechanical pull.

terms.d: A device that converts the pressure variations of a sound wave into variations in an electric current.
A device that converts variations in an electric current into pressure variations in the air (sound) using the motor effect.
Small loudspeakers worn on the ears that work in the same way, using the motor effect to vibrate a diaphragm.
A thin, light, flexible sheet in a microphone that vibrates when sound waves hit it.
The light paper or plastic part of a loudspeaker attached to the coil, which vibrates and pushes the air.
Many turns of insulated wire attached to the diaphragm or cone and sitting in a magnetic field.
A magnet that produces its own steady magnetic field; provides the field the coil moves in.
The production of a potential difference across a conductor when it moves relative to a magnetic field (or the field around it changes).
The p.d. produced across a conductor by electromagnetic induction; it causes a current if the circuit is complete.
A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force.
A current that repeatedly changes direction.
The changes between high pressure (compressions) and low pressure (rarefactions) in a sound wave.
The number of vibrations or waves per second, measured in hertz (Hz); sets the pitch of a sound.
The maximum displacement from the rest position; a larger amplitude gives a louder sound or larger signal.
A device that increases the amplitude of an electrical signal without changing its frequency.
A device that converts a signal from one form to another, such as sound to electrical.

mistakes.w: The loudspeaker uses electromagnetic induction to make sound.
mistakes.r: A loudspeaker uses the motor effect: the current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a force.

mistakes.w: The microphone uses the motor effect.
mistakes.r: A microphone uses electromagnetic induction: the moving coil cuts magnetic field lines and a p.d. is induced.

mistakes.w: The sound waves create electricity in the magnet.
mistakes.r: The p.d. is induced in the coil, which moves relative to the magnet's field.

mistakes.w: The diaphragm vibrates and this makes a current.
mistakes.r: The diaphragm moves the attached coil in the magnetic field; the coil cuts field lines, inducing a p.d. and so a current.

mistakes.w: The magnet vibrates in the microphone.
mistakes.r: In a moving-coil microphone the coil moves; the permanent magnet stays still.

mistakes.w: A loudspeaker works with direct current.
mistakes.r: It needs alternating (varying) current so the force reverses and the cone vibrates back and forth.

mistakes.w: The current has a different frequency from the sound.
mistakes.r: The current has the same frequency as the sound wave (and the loudspeaker cone vibrates at the same frequency as the current).

mistakes.w: Louder sound means faster current.
mistakes.r: Louder sound means larger amplitude vibrations, so a larger induced p.d. and current.

exam.q: Name the effect used by a moving-coil microphone to produce a current.
model: Electromagnetic induction (generator effect)
exam.tip: One word answer is fine, but 'induction' alone needs 'electromagnetic' to be safe.

exam.q: Name the effect that makes the coil of a loudspeaker move.
model: The motor effect
exam.tip: Do not confuse with induction.

exam.q: State the energy transfer in a microphone.
model: Sound (kinetic energy of vibrating air) to electrical energy
exam.tip: Order matters: input first.

exam.q: Explain why the current from a microphone is alternating.
model: The coil moves backwards and forwards / vibrates
So the direction of the induced p.d. (current) reverses each time the coil changes direction
exam.tip: Link the reversal of motion to the reversal of current.

exam.q: A microphone picks up a sound of frequency 500 Hz. State the frequency of the current produced and explain why.
model: 500 Hz
The coil vibrates at the same frequency as the diaphragm / sound wave
exam.tip: Frequency is unchanged through microphone, amplifier and loudspeaker.

exam.q: Explain why a loudspeaker connected to a d.c. supply does not produce a continuous sound.
model: Direct current gives a force in one direction only
So the cone moves once and does not vibrate (no pressure variations)
exam.tip: Mention lack of vibration explicitly.

exam.q: Explain how increasing the current in a loudspeaker coil affects the sound.
model: Larger current gives a larger force on the coil
Cone vibrates with larger amplitude so the sound is louder
exam.tip: Force is proportional to current (F = BIl).

exam.q: Explain how a louder sound changes the output of a microphone.
model: Larger pressure variations make the diaphragm / coil move further and faster
Coil cuts field lines faster so a larger p.d. / current is induced
exam.tip: Amplitude, not frequency, changes.

exam.q: Describe how a loudspeaker produces sound from an alternating current.
model: Alternating current flows in the coil in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet
A force acts on the coil (motor effect)
The force reverses when the current reverses so the coil and cone vibrate
The cone pushes the air producing compressions and rarefactions / sound waves of the same frequency
exam.tip: Four steps, four marks: current, force, reversal, sound.

exam.q: Explain how a moving-coil microphone converts the pressure variations in a sound wave into variations in current.
model: Pressure variations make the diaphragm vibrate
The coil attached to the diaphragm moves in the magnetic field of the magnet
The coil cuts field lines so a p.d. is induced (electromagnetic induction)
The induced current varies / alternates with the same frequency as the sound
exam.tip: Name the coil and the magnetic field.

exam.q: A microphone is connected through an amplifier to a loudspeaker. Explain how a sound made at the microphone is reproduced by the loudspeaker. (6 marks)
model: Sound wave pressure variations make the microphone diaphragm and coil vibrate
Coil moves in magnetic field and cuts field lines
p.d. / alternating current is induced that varies with the same frequency as the sound
Amplifier increases the size of the current
In the loudspeaker the alternating current in the coil in a magnetic field experiences a force (motor effect) that reverses as current reverses
Coil and cone vibrate, producing pressure variations / sound waves of the same frequency
exam.tip: Structure as two chains joined by the amplifier; use the words induced and motor effect.

worked.q: Model answer (4 marks): Explain how headphones produce sound.
steps: Headphones contain a coil attached to a thin diaphragm, in the field of a permanent magnet.
An alternating current from the device flows through the coil.
The current-carrying coil in the magnetic field experiences a force (motor effect).
As the current changes direction the force changes direction, so the coil and diaphragm vibrate at the frequency of the current.
The vibrating diaphragm creates pressure variations in the air: a sound wave.
worked.ans: Alternating current in the coil, force from the motor effect that reverses, diaphragm vibrates, sound waves of the same frequency.

worked.q: Applied example: A singer moves from a quiet low note to a loud high note in front of a microphone. Describe two changes to the current produced.
steps: Higher note = higher frequency sound, so the diaphragm and coil vibrate more times per second.
So the induced alternating current has a higher frequency.
Louder note = larger pressure variations, so the coil moves further and faster through the field.
The coil cuts field lines faster, so a larger p.d. is induced and the current has a larger amplitude.
worked.ans: The current alternates at a higher frequency and has a larger amplitude (peak value).

worked.q: Applied example: Explain why speaking into a loudspeaker connected to a sensitive meter makes the meter needle flicker.
steps: The sound waves make the cone vibrate.
The coil attached to the cone moves in the magnetic field of the magnet.
The coil cuts field lines, so a p.d. is induced (electromagnetic induction) and a small current flows.
The coil moves back and forth, so the current keeps changing direction and size: the needle flickers.
worked.ans: The loudspeaker acts as a microphone: induction produces a small alternating current.

phy_edx.12.4.summary: A **transformer** is two coils of insulated wire, the **primary** and the **secondary**, wound on the same **iron core**. An **alternating current** in the primary coil produces a **changing magnetic field** in the core, and this changing field passing through the secondary coil **induces an alternating potential difference** across it, so a current flows in any circuit connected to it. Because the induced p.d. depends on the number of turns, a transformer can **change the size of an alternating voltage**: step-up transformers increase it and step-down transformers decrease it. Transformers only work with a.c.

core.p: Edexcel 13.5 and 13.6 (all students) ask you to **explain how an alternating current in one circuit can induce a current in another circuit in a transformer**, and to **recall that a transformer can change the size of an alternating voltage**.
bullets: Know the **structure**: primary coil, secondary coil, iron core
Explain the **sequence**: a.c. in primary, changing field in core, changing field through secondary, induced p.d., induced current
Explain **why a.c. is needed** (d.c. does not work)
Recall that a transformer **changes the size of an alternating voltage** (step-up or step-down)

callouts.p: A transformer can change the size of an alternating voltage. It does not work with direct current.

core.p: A basic transformer has two separate coils of **insulated wire** wrapped around a shared **core** made of **iron**. The two coils are **not electrically connected**: no current flows from one coil to the other through a wire. The only link between them is the **magnetic field** in the core.
bullets: **Primary coil**: connected to the **input** a.c. supply
**Secondary coil**: connected to the **output** circuit (the load)
**Iron core**: links the two coils magnetically
Wire is **insulated** so current flows round the turns, not across them or into the core
The number of turns on each coil is chosen to give the output p.d. needed

core.h: Step 1: a.c. in the primary makes a changing field
core.p: A current in a coil produces a magnetic field, just like an electromagnet. Because the supply is **alternating**, the current keeps changing size and reversing direction, so the magnetic field it produces also keeps **changing in size and direction**.
bullets: Current in a coil produces a **magnetic field** (the coil is a solenoid)
Iron core is **magnetised** by this field, making it much **stronger**
a.c. means the current **rises, falls and reverses** many times a second (50 Hz in the UK mains)
So the field in the core is **constantly changing** (alternating)

core.h: Step 2: the core carries the field to the secondary
core.p: The iron core forms a closed loop through both coils. The magnetic field produced by the primary is concentrated in the iron and passes round the core, so it also passes through the secondary coil.
bullets: Iron is a **magnetic material**: it is easily magnetised and concentrates the field lines
Almost all of the field from the primary **passes through the secondary** coil
Without the core, much of the field would spread out into the air and be wasted
The core links the coils **magnetically**, not electrically

callouts.p: Current does NOT flow through the iron core from one coil to the other. The coils are insulated; only the magnetic field is shared.

core.h: Step 3: the changing field induces a p.d. in the secondary
core.p: This is **electromagnetic induction**. When the magnetic field through a coil **changes**, a **potential difference is induced** across the coil. Here nothing physically moves: the field itself is changing, which has the same effect as moving a magnet in and out of the coil.
bullets: Changing field through the secondary = field lines effectively **cutting** the secondary turns
An **alternating p.d. is induced** across the secondary coil
If the secondary is part of a **complete circuit**, an **alternating current** flows in it
The induced p.d. has the **same frequency** as the supply to the primary
More turns on the secondary = a larger induced p.d. (each turn adds a bit)

callouts.p: Electromagnetic induction: a potential difference is induced across a conductor when the magnetic field through it changes (or when it moves relative to a magnetic field).

core.p: Induction only happens while the magnetic field is **changing**. A steady direct current gives a **steady** magnetic field, so after the moment it is switched on there is no change and no p.d. is induced in the secondary.
bullets: **a.c.**: field changes continuously, so a p.d. is induced **all the time**
**d.c.**: field is constant, so **no p.d.** is induced (except a brief pulse when switching on or off)
This is one of the main reasons the **mains supply and National Grid use a.c.**
Exam phrase: 'a changing magnetic field is needed to induce a p.d.'

core.h: Transformers change the size of an alternating voltage
core.p: Because the induced p.d. depends on the number of turns, the output p.d. can be bigger or smaller than the input p.d. This is the key fact to recall from 13.6.
bullets: **Step-up transformer**: **more turns on the secondary** than the primary, output p.d. **greater** than input p.d.
**Step-down transformer**: **fewer turns on the secondary** than the primary, output p.d. **smaller** than input p.d.
Same number of turns: output p.d. **equals** input p.d. (an isolating transformer)
A transformer changes **voltage**, not **frequency**: input and output have the same frequency

callouts.p: Step-UP = UP the turns on the secondary = UP the voltage.
