core.p: A transformer cannot create energy. If it steps the voltage up, the current in the secondary must be smaller than in the primary so that the power output is no greater than the power input. (The power equation is covered in 13.10.)
bullets: Step-up: **voltage increases, current decreases**
Step-down: **voltage decreases, current increases**
For an ideal (100% efficient) transformer, **power in = power out**
Real transformers are very efficient but some energy is wasted as **heating** of the coils and core

core.h: Why the core is made of iron
core.p: The core is made of **soft iron** because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised. With a.c. the field reverses 100 times a second (50 Hz), so the core must be able to follow these rapid changes.
bullets: **Easily magnetised**: makes the field much stronger
**Easily demagnetised** (soft magnetic material): the field can reverse quickly and keep up with the a.c.
**Concentrates** the field and guides it through the secondary coil
A **steel** (permanently magnetisable) core would not work well, because it stays magnetised
Cores are usually built from thin insulated **layers (laminations)** to reduce energy wasted by heating

core.p: Energy is transferred from the primary circuit to the secondary circuit by the **magnetic field**, even though the circuits are not connected by any wire.
bullets: Electrical energy in the primary circuit
Stored and carried in the **changing magnetic field** of the core
Transferred electrically to the secondary circuit by the **induced current**
Some energy is dissipated as **thermal energy** in the coils (resistance) and the core, which is why large transformers are cooled
Less waste means the transformer is closer to 100% efficient

core.p: Transformers are everywhere that a.c. has to be changed to a different voltage. Questions often give an everyday context and ask you to say whether a step-up or step-down transformer is needed.
bullets: **National Grid**: step-up at power stations (to around 400 kV), step-down near homes (to 230 V)
**Phone and laptop chargers**: step-down from 230 V mains to a few volts (then changed to d.c.)
**Doorbells, model railways, halogen lamps**: step-down to a safe low voltage
**Microwave ovens, old TVs**: step-up to thousands of volts
If the device needs a **lower** voltage than the supply, use a **step-down** transformer

core.p: For a 4 to 6 mark 'explain how a transformer works' question, write the chain in order using the key words. Each sentence below is usually one marking point.
bullets: An **alternating current** flows in the **primary coil**
This produces a **changing (alternating) magnetic field** in the **iron core**
The core carries the changing field **through the secondary coil**
The changing field **induces an alternating potential difference** across the secondary coil
If the secondary is connected in a **complete circuit**, an **alternating current** flows
The size of the output p.d. depends on the **number of turns** on the secondary compared with the primary

callouts.p: Use 'changing magnetic field' and 'induced'. Answers that say 'the current travels through the core' get no credit.

analogy.p: Imagine two people holding the same skipping rope over a pulley. One person (the primary) shakes their end up and down; the rope (the iron core) carries the movement across, and the other person's hand (the secondary) is shaken too, even though the two people never touch. If the first person just holds the rope still (d.c.), nothing reaches the other end. Where it breaks down: the rope carries a mechanical wave, whereas a transformer carries a changing magnetic field, and a rope cannot make the second person's movement bigger the way extra secondary turns increase the voltage.

terms.d: A device made of two coils of wire on an iron core that changes the size of an alternating voltage.
The input coil of a transformer, connected to the alternating supply.
The output coil of a transformer, in which an alternating p.d. is induced.
The soft iron frame that links the two coils and concentrates the changing magnetic field.
A material such as iron that is easily magnetised and easily loses its magnetism.
The production of a potential difference across a conductor when the magnetic field through it changes or it moves relative to a field.
The p.d. produced across a coil by a changing magnetic field.
The current that flows when an induced p.d. acts in a complete circuit.
Current that repeatedly reverses direction; UK mains a.c. has a frequency of 50 Hz.
Current that flows in one direction only; gives a steady magnetic field, so cannot work a transformer.
A transformer with more turns on the secondary than the primary, so the output p.d. is larger than the input p.d.
A transformer with fewer turns on the secondary than the primary, so the output p.d. is smaller than the input p.d.
The number of times the wire is wrapped around the core in a coil.
The region around a magnet or current-carrying wire where a magnetic material or moving charge experiences a force.
The fraction of the input energy that is usefully transferred; an ideal transformer is 100% efficient.

mistakes.w: Current flows from the primary coil through the core to the secondary coil.
mistakes.r: The coils are not electrically connected; the changing magnetic field in the core induces a p.d. in the secondary.

mistakes.w: A transformer works on d.c. or batteries.
mistakes.r: Transformers need a.c.; a steady d.c. gives a constant field, so no p.d. is induced.

mistakes.w: The magnetic field induces a current (without saying it changes).
mistakes.r: It must be a CHANGING (alternating) magnetic field that induces the p.d.

mistakes.w: The core is made of copper / steel.
mistakes.r: The core is made of (soft) iron, which is easily magnetised and demagnetised.

mistakes.w: A step-up transformer increases the power / energy.
mistakes.r: It increases the voltage but decreases the current; the power output cannot exceed the power input.

mistakes.w: A step-up transformer has more turns on the primary.
mistakes.r: A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary.

mistakes.w: A transformer changes a.c. into d.c.
mistakes.r: A transformer changes the size of an alternating voltage; the output is still a.c. at the same frequency.

mistakes.w: The primary coil induces a voltage in the core which flows to the secondary.
mistakes.r: The primary current magnetises the core; the changing field passing through the secondary induces the p.d. in the secondary.

exam.q: State what a transformer is used to do.
model: Change the size of an alternating voltage (p.d.)
exam.tip: Include 'alternating'.

exam.q: Name the material used for the core of a transformer.
model: (Soft) iron
exam.tip: Not steel, not copper.

exam.q: State how the number of turns on the coils of a step-down transformer compare.
model: Fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil
exam.tip: Name which coil has fewer turns.

exam.q: Explain why a transformer will not work with a direct current supply.
model: d.c. produces a constant / unchanging magnetic field
A p.d. is only induced when the magnetic field (through the secondary) changes
exam.tip: Two marks: steady field, and induction needs change.

exam.q: Explain why the core of a transformer is made of iron.
model: Iron is easily magnetised (and demagnetised)
So it concentrates / links the changing magnetic field through the secondary coil
exam.tip: Link the property to the job it does.

exam.q: A transformer has a 230 V a.c. input and a 12 V output. State whether it is step-up or step-down and give a reason.
model: Step-down
Output voltage is less than input voltage (so fewer turns on secondary)
exam.tip: Give the reason from the data.

exam.q: State and explain what happens to the current when a transformer steps up the voltage.
model: The current decreases (output current smaller than input current)
Because power output cannot be more than power input / energy is conserved
exam.tip: Voltage up, current down.

exam.q: The primary and secondary coils of a transformer are not connected by any wire. Explain how energy is transferred from the primary circuit to the secondary circuit.
model: Alternating current in primary produces a changing magnetic field
Field passes through the iron core to the secondary coil
Changing field induces a p.d. / current in the secondary coil
exam.tip: Energy is carried by the magnetic field.

exam.q: Explain how an alternating current in the primary coil of a transformer causes a current in the secondary circuit.
model: Alternating current in primary coil produces a magnetic field that is changing / alternating
The iron core carries / concentrates this field through the secondary coil
The changing magnetic field induces an alternating p.d. across the secondary coil
Which causes a current in the secondary if it is part of a complete circuit
exam.tip: Key words: changing field, iron core, induced, complete circuit.

exam.q: A student connects a 6 V battery to the primary coil of a transformer and a lamp to the secondary. The lamp flashes briefly when the switch is closed but then stays off. Explain these observations.
model: When switched on the current rises so the magnetic field changes, inducing a brief p.d. / current in the secondary (lamp flashes)
After that the current is steady so the magnetic field is constant
No change in field means no induced p.d., so the lamp stays off
exam.tip: Link each observation to whether the field is changing.

exam.q: Describe the structure of a transformer and explain how it can be used to produce an output voltage greater than its input voltage. (6 marks)
model: Two coils of insulated wire (primary and secondary) wound on an iron core
Alternating current / p.d. supplied to the primary coil
Produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core
Changing field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating p.d.
For a larger output the secondary coil has more turns than the primary (step-up)
Output is still a.c. of the same frequency; current in secondary is smaller
exam.tip: Cover structure, mechanism and the turns condition.

worked.q: Applied example: A laptop charger plugs into the 230 V mains and supplies 19 V. A power station generator produces 25 kV which is sent along the National Grid at 400 kV. State the type of transformer needed in each case and which coil has more turns.
steps: Charger: 230 V in, 19 V out, output smaller than input, so step-down.
Step-down means fewer turns on the secondary, so the primary has more turns.
Power station: 25 kV in, 400 kV out, output larger than input, so step-up.
Step-up means more turns on the secondary.
worked.ans: Charger: step-down (more turns on primary). Power station: step-up (more turns on secondary).

worked.q: Model answer (4 marks): Explain how a transformer can light a lamp connected only to its secondary coil.
steps: An alternating current flows in the primary coil connected to the a.c. supply.
This produces a changing magnetic field which is concentrated in the iron core.
The changing magnetic field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating p.d. across it.
The lamp completes the secondary circuit, so an induced alternating current flows through the lamp and lights it.
worked.ans: a.c. in primary, changing field in iron core, induced p.d. in secondary, current through the lamp.

worked.q: Applied example: The primary coil of a transformer is connected to a 50 Hz a.c. supply. Describe the frequency and type of the output, and what would change if the secondary coil were given more turns.
steps: The induced p.d. follows the changing field, which changes at the supply frequency.
So the output is alternating at 50 Hz.
More turns on the secondary means each turn adds its own induced p.d.
So the output p.d. would be larger, but the frequency would still be 50 Hz.
worked.ans: The output is a.c. at 50 Hz; more secondary turns gives a larger output p.d. at the same frequency.

phy_edx.12.5.summary: The **turns ratio equation** links the voltages across the two coils of a transformer to their numbers of turns: **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns**, where p is the primary (input) coil and s is the secondary (output) coil. The ratio of the voltages equals the ratio of the turns, so the output voltage is **directly proportional** to the number of secondary turns. Triple students must be able to rearrange it to find either a **missing voltage** or a **missing number of turns**, and use it to decide whether a transformer is step-up or step-down.

core.p: Edexcel 13.7P (triple only) says: **use the turns ratio equation for transformers to calculate either the missing voltage or the missing number of turns**. The equation is given on the Physics equation sheet, but you must be able to substitute, rearrange and give units confidently.
bullets: Equation: **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns**
Find a missing **voltage** (Vp or Vs)
Find a missing **number of turns** (Np or Ns)
Use the ratio to decide **step-up or step-down**

callouts.p: potential difference across primary coil / potential difference across secondary coil = number of turns on primary coil / number of turns on secondary coil.  Vp / Vs = Np / Ns

core.p: There are only two kinds of quantity in this equation, and the units of each pair cancel, so the ratios have no units.
bullets: **Vp** = potential difference (voltage) across the **primary** coil, in volts (V)
**Vs** = potential difference across the **secondary** coil, in volts (V)
**Np** = number of turns on the primary coil (just a number, **no unit**)
**Ns** = number of turns on the secondary coil (no unit)
Vp and Vs must be in the **same unit** (both V, or both kV) because they appear as a ratio

core.p: Each turn of wire on the core experiences the same changing magnetic field, so each turn has the same p.d. induced across it (the 'volts per turn'). The total p.d. across a coil is the volts per turn multiplied by the number of turns. That is why the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio.
bullets: Volts per turn is the **same on both coils**: Vp / Np = Vs / Ns
Double the secondary turns and you **double** the output voltage
Vs is **directly proportional** to Ns (for fixed Vp and Np)
Vs is **directly proportional** to Vp (for fixed turns)
Vs is **inversely proportional** to Np (for fixed Vp and Ns)

callouts.p: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np is the same equation flipped. Either is correct, as long as both sides are flipped together.

core.h: Step-up or step-down from the ratio
core.p: You can tell the type of transformer just by comparing the turns, without calculating anything.
bullets: **Ns greater than Np**: Vs greater than Vp, **step-up**
**Ns less than Np**: Vs less than Vp, **step-down**
**Ns equal to Np**: Vs equals Vp (no change)
A turns ratio Np : Ns of **1 : 20** steps the voltage **up** 20 times
A turns ratio Np : Ns of **20 : 1** steps the voltage **down** to one twentieth

core.p: Cross-multiplying gives **Vp x Ns = Vs x Np**, from which any one quantity can be made the subject. Learn this cross-multiplied form: it avoids mistakes.
bullets: **Vs = Vp x Ns / Np** (find output voltage)
**Vp = Vs x Np / Ns** (find input voltage)
**Ns = Np x Vs / Vp** (find secondary turns)
**Np = Ns x Vp / Vs** (find primary turns)
Check: the unknown is always on top of one fraction after rearranging

callouts.p: Write Vp x Ns = Vs x Np, then divide both sides by whatever is multiplied by the unknown.

core.p: Examiners give marks for substitution and for the answer, so show each step clearly.
bullets: 1. **Write down** the equation: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
2. **List** the values with their symbols; make sure p and s are matched correctly
3. **Convert** so Vp and Vs are in the same unit (e.g. both in V)
4. **Substitute** the numbers into the equation
5. **Rearrange** and calculate
6. **Give units** for a voltage (V); turns have no unit, and should be a **whole number**
7. **Sense check**: step-up means Vs bigger than Vp and Ns bigger than Np

core.p: The most common question. Usually you are given the input voltage and both numbers of turns and asked for the output voltage.
bullets: Example: Vp = 230 V, Np = 2000, Ns = 100
Vs = Vp x Ns / Np = 230 x 100 / 2000
Ns is less than Np, so it is step-down: an answer smaller than 230 V makes sense

core.h: Finding a missing number of turns
core.p: Here you are given both voltages and one number of turns. The answer is a count of loops of wire, so it should be a whole number and has no unit.
bullets: Example: Vp = 12 V, Vs = 240 V, Np = 50
Ns = Np x Vs / Vp = 50 x 240 / 12
Ns = **1000 turns**
Vs is 20 times Vp, so Ns must be 20 times Np: 20 x 50 = 1000, consistent

callouts.p: Do not write a unit such as V or A after a number of turns. Write 'turns' or no unit.

core.h: Working with kV and large numbers
core.p: National Grid questions use kilovolts (kV). 1 kV = 1000 V. Because the equation uses a ratio, you can leave both voltages in kV, but you must not mix kV and V.
bullets: Convert both to V, or keep both in kV
Example: Vp = 25 kV, Vs = 400 kV, Np = 1500: Ns = 1500 x 400 / 25 = **24 000 turns**
Mixing units (25 kV with 230 V) without converting gives an answer 1000 times too big or small
Standard form may help with large turn numbers

core.p: Often the numbers are chosen so that you can spot the scale factor. Finding it first is quick and makes errors obvious.
bullets: Find how many times bigger (or smaller) the secondary is: **Ns / Np**
Multiply Vp by the same factor to get Vs
Example: Np = 400, Ns = 40: factor = 40 / 400 = 0.1, so 230 V becomes **23 V**
Example: Vp = 6 V, Vs = 30 V: factor 5, so Ns = 5 x Np

core.p: The turns ratio equation gives the output of an **ideal** transformer. Real transformers are very efficient, so the equation is a very good prediction, but a measured Vs is usually slightly lower than predicted.
bullets: Assumes all the magnetic field from the primary passes through the secondary
Assumes no energy wasted by **heating** of the coils or core
The equation applies to **alternating** voltages only (transformers do not work on d.c.)
The **frequency** is unchanged; only the size of the voltage changes
Linked equation (13.10): for 100% efficiency, **Vp x Ip = Vs x Is**, so stepping up the voltage steps down the current by the same factor

core.p: Higher marks come from questions that join the turns ratio equation to another idea, such as the power equation or choosing a transformer.
bullets: Find Vs with the turns ratio, then the current with Vp x Ip = Vs x Is
Choose which of several transformers gives the voltage needed for a device
Explain why a student's measured Vs is lower than calculated (energy losses, not 100% efficient)
Calculate the turns needed to step up for transmission and then down again for homes

callouts.p: If a question gives turns and voltages for both coils and asks 'is the transformer ideal?', calculate the predicted Vs and compare with the measured value.

analogy.p: Think of each turn of wire as one step on a staircase, and every step is exactly the same height (the volts per turn, set by the changing field in the core). The primary coil has Np steps adding up to height Vp; the secondary has Ns steps of the same height, so its total height is Vs. More steps means more height, in exact proportion. Where it breaks down: the 'step height' is not fixed by the stairs themselves but by the input voltage and primary turns, and stairs do not need anything to keep changing, whereas a transformer only works while the magnetic field is alternating.

terms.d: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns: the ratio of primary to secondary voltage equals the ratio of primary to secondary turns.
The ratio of the number of turns on the primary coil to the number on the secondary coil, Np : Ns.
The input coil of a transformer, connected to the a.c. supply.
The output coil of a transformer, across which an alternating p.d. is induced.
The potential difference across the primary coil, measured in volts (V).
The potential difference across the secondary coil, measured in volts (V).
The number of turns of wire on the primary coil (no unit).
The number of turns of wire on the secondary coil (no unit).
A transformer with Ns greater than Np, so that Vs is greater than Vp.
A transformer with Ns less than Np, so that Vs is less than Vp.
Two quantities are directly proportional if doubling one doubles the other; Vs is directly proportional to Ns.
1000 volts.
A transformer assumed to be 100% efficient, with no energy wasted, so power in equals power out.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts (V).

mistakes.w: Vs = Vp x Np / Ns
mistakes.r: Vs = Vp x Ns / Np: the output voltage increases with the number of SECONDARY turns.

mistakes.w: Mixing p and s, e.g. Vp / Vs = Ns / Np
mistakes.r: Keep primary with primary: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns (or Vs / Vp = Ns / Np).

mistakes.w: Using 25 kV and 230 V directly in the ratio.
mistakes.r: Convert to the same unit first (25 000 V and 230 V) before substituting.

mistakes.w: Answer for turns given as 1000 V or with a decimal like 333.3 turns without comment.
mistakes.r: Turns have no unit and are a whole number; round sensibly (e.g. 333 turns).

mistakes.w: A step-up transformer has more primary turns.
mistakes.r: A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary (Ns greater than Np).

mistakes.w: Using the turns ratio to calculate current as if current is proportional to turns.
mistakes.r: Current goes the opposite way: Is / Ip = Np / Ns for an ideal transformer, from Vp x Ip = Vs x Is.

mistakes.w: A step-down answer bigger than the input voltage, accepted without checking.
mistakes.r: Always sense check: step-down means Vs must be less than Vp.

mistakes.w: The equation works for a battery (d.c.) input.
mistakes.r: Transformers and the turns ratio equation only apply to alternating voltages.

exam.q: Write down the equation linking the potential differences across the coils of a transformer and the numbers of turns on the coils.
model: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns (or equivalent)
exam.tip: Symbols must be defined or words used.

exam.q: A transformer has 200 turns on the primary coil and 50 turns on the secondary coil. State whether it is step-up or step-down.
model: Step-down (fewer turns on secondary)
exam.tip: Compare Ns with Np.

exam.q: A transformer has a turns ratio Np : Ns of 1 : 10. The input voltage is 23 V. Calculate the output voltage.
model: Vs = 230 V
exam.tip: Scale factor shortcut.

exam.q: The primary coil of a transformer has 1200 turns and the secondary has 60 turns. The input voltage is 230 V. Calculate the output voltage.
exam.tip: Show the substitution for the method marks.

exam.q: A transformer changes 230 V to 6 V. The primary coil has 1150 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil.
model: Ns = 30 (turns)
exam.tip: No unit for turns.

exam.q: A transformer steps up 400 V to 132 kV. The secondary coil has 33 000 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the primary coil.
model: Np = 100 (turns)
exam.tip: Convert kV first.

exam.q: A student calculates that the output of a transformer should be 12.0 V, but measures 11.4 V. Suggest why.
model: The transformer is not 100% efficient / not ideal
Energy is wasted (heating the coils / core) or not all the magnetic field links the secondary
exam.tip: The equation assumes an ideal transformer.

exam.q: Explain, using the turns ratio, why a transformer with more turns on its secondary coil than on its primary coil produces a larger output voltage.
model: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np so if Ns is greater than Np then Vs is greater than Vp
Each turn has the same induced p.d., so more turns give a larger total p.d.
exam.tip: Volts per turn idea is grade 9.

exam.q: An ideal transformer has Np = 500 and Ns = 25. The input is 240 V and the input current is 0.10 A. Calculate the output voltage and the output current.
model: Vs = 12 V
Vp x Ip = Vs x Is so 240 x 0.10 = 12 x Is
Is = 2.0 A
exam.tip: Voltage down by 20, current up by 20.

exam.q: A model railway needs 12 V from the 230 V mains. A student has a transformer core, a primary coil of 920 turns, and wire to make a secondary coil. Describe how the student should choose the number of secondary turns, including a calculation, and how they could check the transformer works. (6 marks)
model: Use Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
Ns = Np x Vs / Vp = 920 x 12 / 230
Ns = 48 turns
Secondary has fewer turns than primary so it is a step-down transformer
Connect primary to a.c. (not d.c.) supply
Measure output with a voltmeter across the secondary; expect slightly less than 12 V because the transformer is not 100% efficient
exam.tip: Combine calculation with practical sense.

worked.q: A phone charger transformer has 1150 turns on its primary coil and 60 turns on its secondary coil. It is connected to the 230 V mains. Calculate the output voltage.
steps: Equation: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
Values: Vp = 230 V, Np = 1150, Ns = 60
Rearrange: Vs = Vp x Ns / Np
Calculate: Vs = 12 V
Check: Ns is less than Np, so step-down, and 12 V is less than 230 V. Correct.

worked.q: A power station transformer steps up 25 kV to 400 kV. The primary coil has 500 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil.
steps: Equation: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
Both voltages in kV: Vp = 25 kV, Vs = 400 kV (same unit, so no conversion needed)
Rearrange: Ns = Np x Vs / Vp
Substitute: Ns = 500 x 400 / 25
Calculate: Ns = 8000
Check: voltage up 16 times, so turns up 16 times: 16 x 500 = 8000.

worked.q: A doorbell needs 5.0 V. Its transformer has 40 turns on the secondary and runs from 230 V. Calculate the number of turns on the primary coil.
steps: Equation: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
Values: Vp = 230 V, Vs = 5.0 V, Ns = 40
Cross-multiply: Vp x Ns = Vs x Np
Rearrange: Np = Vp x Ns / Vs = 230 x 40 / 5.0
Calculate: Np = 9200 / 5.0 = 1840
Check: step-down, so Np should be bigger than Ns. 1840 is bigger than 40.
